USA-washington-d-c: A diamond of land deliberately carved out of two states so no state could own the capital — the Potomac cuts the diamond's southwest edge.
USA-new-york: The harbor at the Hudson's mouth made it the front door of America — a fifth of all Americans can trace an ancestor through Ellis Island here.
USA-los-angeles: A desert coast with no natural harbor or river — the second-largest US city runs entirely on water piped hundreds of miles over mountains.
USA-chicago: Sits on the one low spot between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi basin — every railroad had to pass it, so it became the crossroads of the continent.
USA-miami: The only major US city conjured from a tropical swamp — it sits barely two meters above a rising sea, on the continent's southeastern tip.
CAN-ottawa: Chosen by Queen Victoria partly because it was a safe distance from the American border — unlike nearly every other Canadian city.
CAN-toronto: A third of Canadians live within a two-hour drive of it, all crowded onto Lake Ontario's northwest shore.
CAN-montreal: An island city in the St. Lawrence River, and the world's second-largest French-speaking city after Paris.
MEX-mexico-city: Built on a drained lake bed at 2,240m — the city is sinking up to half a meter a year into the old lake floor.
MEX-guadalajara: Mexico's second city, inland and west — the home of mariachi and, in the agave fields around it, tequila.
MEX-monterrey: Mexico's industrial powerhouse, tucked against the Sierra Madre just two hours' drive from the Texas border.
GTM-guatemala-city: Rebuilt on a plateau after earthquakes flattened the old capital Antigua — still ringed by three active volcanoes.
BLZ-belmopan: One of the world's tiniest capitals, built inland from scratch after Hurricane Hattie drowned coastal Belize City in 1961.
HND-tegucigalpa: A former silver-mining camp crammed into a mountain bowl — its airport approach between peaks was long rated the world's scariest.
SLV-san-salvador: Sits directly beneath its own volcano in the 'Valley of the Hammocks' — swung by earthquakes so often the nickname stuck.
NIC-managua: Placed on Lake Managua's shore as a compromise between feuding León and Granada — earthquakes leveled it twice, so its 'downtown' is still scattered.
CRI-san-jose: A coffee-boom capital on a mile-high plateau — the beans grown on the surrounding volcano slopes paid for its opera house.
PAN-panama-city: The only capital where you can watch ocean-going ships queue past skyscrapers — the Pacific mouth of the Canal is its front yard.
BRA-brasilia: Drawn in the shape of an airplane and built in under four years on empty savanna, to drag Brazil's center of gravity inland from the coast.
BRA-sao-paulo: The southern hemisphere's biggest city — a coffee fortune turned into an endless high-rise plateau just uphill from the sea.
BRA-rio-de-janeiro: Its bay was mistaken for a river mouth in January 1502 — hence 'January River' — and Sugarloaf mountain still guards the mistake.
BRA-belo-horizonte: Brazil's first planned city, ringed by the iron mountains of Minas Gerais that feed its steel mills.
BRA-porto-alegre: The industrial south's port, sitting where five rivers merge into a freshwater lagoon near Uruguay.
ARG-buenos-aires: Home to a third of all Argentines, on the bank of the Río de la Plata — a 'river' so wide the far shore in Uruguay is invisible.
COL-bogota: A capital at 2,640m on an Andean plateau — high enough that its climate is an eternal cool spring on the equator.
COL-medellin: Colombia's 'city of eternal spring', filling a narrow Andean valley — its cable cars are public transit up the slopes.
PER-lima: A capital in a desert that almost never rains — it drinks entirely from rivers falling out of the Andes behind it.
VEN-caracas: Squeezed into a mountain valley one ridge back from the Caribbean — its airport sits on the coast, a mountain pass away.
CHL-santiago: Backed by the highest Andes — from downtown you can ski at 3,000m and reach the Pacific, in opposite directions, within two hours.
BOL-sucre: The constitutional capital Bolivia keeps for its courts — government long since moved up to La Paz, 3,600m high.
ECU-quito: The closest capital to the equator line — the monument marking latitude zero stands in its northern suburbs.
PRY-asuncion: One of South America's oldest cities, the river port from which Buenos Aires itself was re-founded downstream.
URY-montevideo: Holds a third of Uruguay on the north shore of the Río de la Plata, staring across at Buenos Aires.
GBR-london: Built at the lowest point the Romans could bridge the Thames — the tide still reaches through the city twice a day.
FRA-paris: Began as a fort on an island in the Seine — every French road distance is still measured from the zero point outside Notre-Dame.
DEU-berlin: Sits far east in Germany — closer to Poland than to most of Germany's own big cities, a legacy of Prussia's eastern heart.
ITA-rome: The Tiber crossing where all roads converged — and the only capital with an entire sovereign state (the Vatican) inside it.
ESP-madrid: Europe's highest major capital, planted dead-center on Spain's plateau by royal decree — chosen precisely for being in the middle.
ESP-barcelona: Spain's Mediterranean door and Catalonia's capital — its street grid breaks into Gaudí's curves near the sea.
PRT-lisbon: Europe's westernmost capital, on the Tagus estuary — the earthquake that destroyed it in 1755 shook European philosophy too.
NLD-amsterdam: A city of 165 canals on wooden piles in a bog — the airport sits four meters below sea level.
GRC-athens: The Acropolis has been continuously in view for 3,400 years — the city fills the basin between it and the sea at Piraeus.
POL-warsaw: Rebuilt brick-by-brick from paintings after being 85% destroyed in 1944 — its 'old town' is a meticulous 1950s reconstruction.
UKR-kyiv: The thousand-year-old city on the Dnipro's bluffs where East Slavic civilization began — golden domes above a river highway.
RUS-moscow: The Kremlin is literally 'the fortress' — the city grew in concentric rings around it, and all Russian highways still radiate from it.
RUS-st-petersburg: Peter the Great's window on Europe, willed out of a Baltic swamp — its summer nights never fully darken.
TUR-ankara: Atatürk moved the capital here, deep in the Anatolian steppe, deliberately turning Turkey's back on imperial Istanbul.
TUR-istanbul: The only city on two continents — the Bosphorus through its middle is the strait between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
CHN-beijing: The 'northern capital' — the Forbidden City at its heart aligns the whole street grid to the compass, as imperial cosmology demanded.
CHN-shanghai: At the mouth of the Yangtze, the river that drains a third of China — the world's busiest container port.
CHN-guangzhou: The Canton of the old trade — for centuries the single port where the West was allowed to buy from China.
CHN-shenzhen: A fishing town of 30,000 in 1980, a metropolis of 17 million now — the fastest city ever built, pressed against Hong Kong.
CHN-wuhan: The crossing where the Yangtze meets China's north–south railways — the country's central junction.
JPN-tokyo: The world's largest metropolis, on the Kanto plain — still officially a collection of villages that fused around Edo castle.
JPN-osaka: Japan's merchant capital and kitchen, on the Inland Sea — the historic rival to samurai Tokyo.
JPN-yokohama: The fishing village opened to foreign ships in 1859 — it grew into Japan's second city, fused to Tokyo's southern edge.
JPN-nagoya: The workshop between Tokyo and Osaka — Toyota's home turf on the Pacific coast's central bay.
KOR-seoul: Half of all South Koreans live in its metro area — barely 50km from the DMZ, within artillery range of the border.
KOR-busan: Korea's southern port, the last redoubt that never fell in the Korean War — now a container gateway facing Japan.
IND-new-delhi: The eighth city built on this site — imperial capitals stack here at the gap between the Thar desert and the Himalaya.
IND-mumbai: Seven islands stitched together by land reclamation — India's financial capital, film industry, and busiest port in one.
IND-kolkata: The British Raj's first capital, in the Ganges delta — the river here is already splitting into the world's largest delta.
IND-chennai: South India's gateway on the Bay of Bengal — the old Madras of the spice-and-cotton coast.
IDN-jakarta: Sinking so fast — up to 25cm a year — that Indonesia is building a replacement capital on Borneo.
THA-bangkok: Its full ceremonial name is 168 letters, a world record — the city sprawls across the Chao Phraya's delta marsh.
VNM-hanoi: The 'city between rivers' in the Red River delta — Vietnam's thousand-year-old northern capital.
VNM-ho-chi-minh-city: Still 'Saigon' to most of its residents — the Mekong delta's metropolis and the old southern capital.
MMR-yangon: The golden Shwedagon pagoda towers over it — Myanmar's generals abandoned it for a purpose-built capital in 2005.
PAK-karachi: Pakistan's port colossus on the Arabian Sea — it was the capital until Islamabad was purpose-built in the north.
PAK-lahore: The Mughal garden city, a stone's throw from the Indian border — the partition line of 1947 runs just east of it.
BGD-chattogram: Bangladesh's port on the Bay of Bengal, where much of the world's shipping goes to die on the breaking beaches nearby.
IRN-tehran: Climbs the slopes of the Alborz mountains — from downtown you look up at a 5,600m volcano between city and Caspian.
IRQ-baghdad: Founded as a perfect circle on the Tigris in 762 — for centuries the largest and most learned city on Earth.
ISR-jerusalem: A hilltop city sacred to three faiths — the walled Old City covers less than one square kilometer.
ISR-tel-aviv: Founded in 1909 on empty dunes north of ancient Jaffa — now Israel's Mediterranean business and beach capital.
SAU-riyadh: A mud-walled oasis town a century ago, now a desert metropolis dead-center in the peninsula.
SAU-jeddah: The Red Sea port that has received Mecca's pilgrims for thirteen centuries — the hajj gateway.
EGY-cairo: The largest city of Africa and the Arab world, pinned to the point where the Nile fans into its delta — pyramids stand in its suburbs.
EGY-alexandria: Alexander's harbor on the delta's western edge — its ancient lighthouse and library were both wonders of the world.
MAR-casablanca: Morocco's Atlantic port and business capital — far bigger than the four royal capitals, and younger than all of them.
NGA-abuja: Built in the 1980s at Nigeria's geographic center, a neutral capital between the Muslim north and Christian south.
NGA-lagos: Africa's largest city, spilling across lagoon islands — projected to be among the world's biggest megacities by 2100.
NGA-kano: The Sahel's ancient trading city — the southern terminus of trans-Saharan caravans for a thousand years.
ETH-addis-ababa: Africa's diplomatic capital at 2,355m — home of the African Union, in highlands cool enough for eucalyptus forests.
KEN-nairobi: Began as a railway supply depot in 1899 — the only capital with a national park (lions included) on its doorstep.
ZAF-pretoria: The executive capital in South Africa's three-capital split — administration here, parliament in Cape Town, courts in Bloemfontein.
ZAF-johannesburg: The world's largest city not on a river, coast, or lake — it exists purely because of the gold reef beneath it.
AUS-canberra: Sydney and Melbourne both refused to let the other be capital, so Australia built one in the bush between them.
AUS-sydney: Wrapped around the drowned river valley of Port Jackson — the harbor the First Fleet chose in 1788.
AUS-melbourne: Australia's southern rival, on Port Phillip Bay — a gold-rush boomtown that was briefly the richest city in the world.
NZL-wellington: The world's southernmost capital, gripping the hills of a strait so windy its nickname is simply 'Windy Wellington'.
